ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with informal pre-meeting chatter followed by much longer, structured presentation turns and brief Q&A exchanges. Participants overlap lightly and often respond with quick acknowledgments such as “yeah,” “okay,” or “great,” while occasional interruptions arise from audio, login, or turn-taking issues. The tone is friendly, collegial, and technically professional but not polished or scripted; speakers use frequent fillers, repetitions, self-corrections, and false starts (“um,” “you know,” repeated words, restarting clauses). Questions are usually prefaced gently—“I have a quick question,” “maybe a naive question,” “do you think”—and often become long, exploratory formulations rather than concise prompts. People build on prior remarks through agreement, praise, and extensions of the speaker’s reasoning; challenges are indirect and framed as curiosity, caveats, or open questions rather than confrontation. Presenters regularly hedge with phrases like “we think,” “likely,” “sort of,” “I would say,” and “as far as we know,” especially when interpreting results or discussing future work.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - So what I keep coming back to, and this is just from the last couple of projects I've run, is that you pay for it later if you skip the pilot, you always do, and then...
  - Mm.
  - Sorry, can I ask- is that the same pilot as the spring one?
Opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Judging whether a headband neurofeedback program improves attention in elementary classrooms.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Patel
speakers.background: Dr. Patel is a cognitive neuroscientist with 9 years of experience designing EEG studies of sustained attention and self-regulation in children. She has worked with mobile and school-based EEG protocols, preprocessing artifact-prone recordings, and preregistered trials of computerized cognitive training. In the proposed pilot, she will help define a small set of prespecified attention-related EEG markers, design procedures to separate neurofeedback-specific effects from expectancy effects, and plan a six-week follow-up assessment.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats the intervention as a test of a plausible neural mechanism rather than assuming that engaging with a headband demonstrates brain change. She wants the study to ask whether neurofeedback produces reliable changes in predefined EEG attention-related markers, whether any gains exceed credible expectancy or placebo explanations, and whether those changes persist after sessions stop. She is wary of relying on broad teacher impressions alone as evidence of mechanism, while recognizing that usable school outcomes are needed for the program to matter.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Morales
speakers.background: Dr. Morales is an educational researcher with 12 years of experience in elementary-school intervention studies and district research partnerships. Her work uses classroom observation protocols, teacher implementation logs, student-reported experience measures, and mixed-methods analyses of instructional feasibility and equity. She has led studies in grades 3–5 involving tiered supports, classroom technology, and accommodations for students with disabilities.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She frames success in terms of whether the program improves attention as it is enacted in ordinary classrooms and whether any change is meaningful for learning-relevant outcomes. She will focus on classroom attention observations, brief student measures, teacher reports, selected learning indicators, implementation fidelity, lesson-time disruption, and participation equity across hair types, sensory needs, disability accommodations, and technology access. She expects effects to be interpreted in relation to local instructional ecology rather than as decontextualized individual performance alone, while deferring to neuroscience colleagues on the validity of particular EEG markers.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Aaron Kim
speakers.background: Dr. Kim is a biomedical engineer and postdoctoral researcher with 5 years of experience evaluating wearable biosensors for pediatric and community settings. He has conducted bench and field testing of dry-electrode EEG systems, including impedance and signal-quality checks, motion-artifact characterization, wireless transfer reliability, battery-life testing, fit assessments, and device-safety documentation. He has collaborated with schools and clinicians to adapt wearable-device procedures for comfort and accessibility.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He approaches the headband as an enabling measurement-and-delivery tool whose performance must be established before substantive study claims can be trusted. He will benchmark dry-electrode recordings against a reference system during a short calibration session, document fit and comfort across children, verify charging and battery performance, inspect wireless data transfer, and complete safety checks before classroom deployment. He will report calibration failure rates and practical device issues as feasibility information, while leaving questions about attention, learning, and child outcomes to the neuroscience and education leads.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: In the meeting, the neuroscientist and education researcher each present a distinct research aim. The neuroscientist says the study should test whether neurofeedback changes prespecified EEG attention-related markers, whether improvements exceed expectancy/placebo effects, and whether changes remain at a six-week follow-up. The education researcher says the study should test whether the program improves classroom attention and learning-relevant outcomes, while examining teacher implementation burden, lesson-time disruption, and equitable participation. The biomedical engineer explains that their role is to validate the dry-electrode headband as a measurement and delivery tool: benchmark signal quality against a reference system during a short calibration session, document fit and comfort across children, verify battery performance, and complete device-safety checks. The engineer does not propose a separate substantive question about attention, learning, or child outcomes. The group decides that neuroscience and education are the two core research areas, while biomedical engineering is an enabling methodological role. The group also agrees that device validation must be completed before the pilot begins and that calibration failure rates will be reported as feasibility data. No final choice is made about the exact EEG marker or the specific learning assessment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I know we only have ten minutes, so maybe today we can just get clear on what would make this a useful pilot. Not only whether the kids can use the headbands, but what evidence would actually persuade us that it changed attention. I’m especially hoping we can talk through the classroom comparison and whether a short calibration can tell us which EEG signal is stable enough to preregister.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: Sorry, I missed the end of the last meeting. Are we still planning a separate short calibration before the ten-week sessions? For me, that needs to establish dry-electrode quality against a reference recording, and also fit and comfort, before we treat any feature as stable enough to preregister. Maya, what threshold would make a recording unusable for your analysis, and how much missingness can you tolerate?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Mm, and comfort too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I’d rather set the cutoff from the calibration data than pretend we know it now, because movement and fit are going to vary a lot from child to child. For a primary EEG analysis, I’d want enough clean data in both the baseline and post session to estimate the same marker reliably. If we’re losing, say, a third of a child’s usable recording, that starts to worry me. But Aaron, I’d need to see what the actual failure pattern looks like first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Losing a third isn't just an analysis problem for us. It may be patterned by hair, sensory tolerance, or who can sit through setup. Aaron, in the calibration, could we record- could we keep fit attempts, adjustment time, and child comfort separate from just a pass-fail signal-quality flag? That would tell us whether the usable-data rule is quietly excluding a particular group.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: I’d log each contact attempt, adjustment time, comfort in a child-friendly rating, whether they stop or decline, and the accommodation used, not fold that into a single failure code. Then we can separate a, a signal problem from a procedure that just isn’t acceptable for that child.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: That separation is really important. Could the comfort and setup log also capture whether the child misses instructional time, and whether an adult has to leave the room or divert the teacher? A technically usable recording could still be pretty infeasible if the routine destabilizes the first fifteen minutes of math.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Yeah, that could really matter.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: I can add timestamps for setup, removal, and when the child returns to the activity, plus whether it pulled in the teacher or another adult. I’d want to distinguish calibration from the regular routine, though. If the reference setup takes longer, that’s not necessarily what the ten-week sessions will cost.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: That distinction makes sense. For the EEG question, though, I'd want the calibration to use the same short, seated routine we can realistically repeat at baseline and post. Not the whole reference setup- otherwise, we may certify a marker under conditions we never have again. And the timestamps will help us see whether the comparison classrooms need some equivalent check-in, because adult attention alone can move a brief task score.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: For the 10-week comparison, I’d make the check-in genuinely equivalent in time and adult contact, but not another attention intervention. Otherwise, otherwise, if teachers later say transitions or on-task behavior changed, we won’t know whether that’s neurofeedback or just a predictable one-to-one routine.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: On the device side, I’d keep the comparison check-in separate from any calibration, because the reference recording is more equipment and more handling than either classroom should get routinely. Elena, could a short, repeatable check-in happen somewhere in the day without taking the child out of the lesson transition? I need to see whether the reference setup is- whether it’s even workable in the available space and time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I don’t know the actual bell schedules yet, so I’d need to check school by school. I’d avoid arrival and the first instructional block entirely. For a ten-week pilot, a fixed midmorning pull-out during independent work or intervention time might be repeatable, although we need to see whether that- whether it ends up differentially taking students from services they need.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I’d be cautious about a fixed pull-out if some children lose intervention time and others don’t, because that itself can affect the outcomes. Could the brief computerized task and the EEG baseline/post be scheduled in the same kind of window for both groups, with the comparison children getting that neutral adult contact? Then, then the second-visit improvement I’ve seen before is less likely to be just practice or being singled out.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: Hm, the window matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: The window also determines what we can call an outcome. If sessions pull children from different kinds of instruction across schools, a ten-week effect on selected learning indicators is going to be almost impossible to interpret. I need to check the grade 3–5 schedules and see if there’s a common non-core slot that isn’t somebody’s mandated service time, because otherwise...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: From the hardware side, I’d rather not assume there’s a common slot until you’ve checked that. The calibration needs a space that’s quiet enough, and some privacy for the reference setup. And the multi-headband wireless transfers drew down batteries faster in the field check than in single-unit bench testing, so I need to test the actual room workflow. Not just whether a slot exists.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: That field workflow test is important because, for a 10-week pilot, a battery or transfer failure isn't just a device issue. It becomes uneven exposure across children. And could you let us know once you've tested the room whether charging and wireless syncing can happen outside the student session window? I lost my- or whether staff would be troubleshooting in front of the class?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: That’s the test I need to run before we promise a classroom workflow. I expect charging can happen overnight and syncing after sessions, but the faster drain under concurrent transfer means I don’t want to assume that. I’ll test several units in the actual room and log whether any staff intervention happens during the student window.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Yeah, and when you test that, could you flag whether failures cluster by classroom or by particular students? If one room has weaker connectivity, or a few children repeatedly lose sessions, the dosage difference could look like an attention effect, or sort of mask one. And teachers will experience that as unreliability, not just missing data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: I can structure the workflow log at both levels, room-level connectivity and transfer failures, then device and session-level battery, sync, and any incomplete delivery. I’m a little wary of calling a missed session a student-specific issue until we know whether it follows the headband, the room, or the timing, but in the field test we should be able to disentangle some of that...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: For the analysis, we should keep the delivered-session count separate from usable EEG minutes. A child might complete every session and still have intermittent signal loss, or they might miss sessions because of a room-level failure. Those mean very different things when we're asking whether a null EEG result is evidence against the mechanism. I'd also want that same log carried through the six-week follow-up, not just the ten weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Right, through follow-up too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: Mm. I can keep that same device and workflow log through the six-week follow-up, including whether a unit was replaced or a session had to be rerun. The main thing I need before I lock the calibration plan is confirmation that the reference system can be set up in whatever school space Elena identifies; if it can’t, I don’t want to imply the benchmark is already solved.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Mm, that’s still an open dependency.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: And before we treat the reference recording as the gatekeeper, I'd want a fallback for children who reasonably can't tolerate it. They shouldn't have to lose access to the classroom-facing outcomes or get coded as nonparticipants because a calibration procedure is burdensome. We can still document feasibility and their attention measures separately. I'll check what spaces and schedules are actually available. Or rather, I'll check whether any of them create a service conflict too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I think that’s the right fallback. We can keep the primary neural-mechanism analysis limited to children with repeatable usable recordings, but that shouldn’t become the definition of whether the program was feasible or helpful in the classroom. And I’d really like to hold the baseline, post, and six-week task procedure constant for everyone, otherwise practice effects are going to be hard to separate from anything else.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I’d keep the classroom observation and teacher report available for every enrolled child at those same points, including children without analyzable EEG. Otherwise we could end up answering whether the headband works for the easiest-to-fit- whether it works only for the easiest-to-fit subgroup, which isn’t really the district’s question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Yeah, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: Yeah—if you find the windows, I’ll confirm the reference setup and, uh, the room workflow before we lock anything in.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I’ll come back with the schedule and space constraints, and I’ll also check which existing learning indicator we can collect across grades without creating another testing block. Then we can see if this is actually— whether it’s implementable, not just technically possible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there. There are a couple of real dependencies to check before we lock the design. I'll follow up by email. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aaron Kim
transcript.text: Thanks, everyone—talk soon.
